rv.q: And I'm thrilled to report that Mrs. Doubtfire: The New Musical Comedy delivered everything I hoped for and more.
MRS. DOUBTFIRE brings big laughs, dazzling quick changes, and plenty of heart to Bass Concert Hall, reminding us that families may change shape while love remains.

The production is driven by Craig Allen Smith, who takes on the dual role of Daniel Hillard and Mrs. Doubtfire. Smith is a whirlwind of energy from the moment the show begins until curtain call. I often say theatre is a sport and Smith proves himself to be an athlete!
It might not be the kind of show that completely changes your perspective on theater, but it's entertaining, nostalgic, and easy to enjoy.
The musical version of the film classic an appropriate and entertaining variation on the universal theme: families come in all shapes, sizes, and colors.
The show taps into the nostalgia of the movie while offering fresh performances and some updates that make it more than just an attempt to capitalize on the film’s fan base.
Ultimately, Mrs. Doubtfire is exactly what it sets out to be: a high-energy, sentimental night of theater.
I left more impressed by what the performers and production team accomplished than by the musical itself.
It’s quite an able cast overall, though —better than community theater quality, but certainly not up to Broadway standards (or even Equity touring).
This production is entertaining, hilarious, and easy to love.
Director Steve Edlund keeps the pace snappy and the energy vibrant throughout the show’s two-hour-and-40-minute running time.

This San Francisco story with homage to Donna Summer really makes for a campy and cute production that still addresses family conflict with love and, humor, compassion, and covers a range of emotions.
Mrs Doubtfire is sometimes a slight misfire, suffering from a weaker book, and a score with no musical source material.
The Mrs. Doubtfire touring production is a well-done, effective, and fun night out at the theater.
Propelled by funny moments and highly entertaining musical numbers, "MRS. DOUBTFIRE" conveys the story of a parent attempting to obtain a deeper understanding of his family…and of himself.
Mrs. Doubtfire is humorous, madcap fun for the entire family, and it’s a stellar addition to the Marcus Performing Arts Center’s Broadway showcase.
It is a vivid, maximalist display of craft that ensures the audience feels every comedic beat and every quiet pang of heartbreak.

Thanks to (some) stand-out acting, strong vocals and lyrics that move the narrative along and give insight into the characters, Mrs. Doubtfire is easy to recommend to even the most die-hard Robin Williams/Harvey Fierstein/Sally Field/Pierce Brosnan fans.
There's no doubt about it: "Mrs. Doubtfire" is a fun evening at the theater.
The musical captures most of the plot of the film through the first act but the longish second half seems padded with too many songs that seem to repeat the same narratives.
All in all, we both enjoyed the show.

Measured as a work of musical theater, however, “Mrs. Doubtfire” falls short in a number of ways, from its forgettable score to its flimsy sets to the cringe-inducing quantity of corn in a sizable chunk of Act One.
If you remember the movie, the musical will stir up forgotten feel-good moments.
The songs (music and lyrics by Wayne Kirkpatrick and Karey Kirkpatrick) are acceptable but instantly forgettable.

cn.t: A fun, nostalgic crowd-pleaser that leans heavily on the beloved film, though critics note a forgettable score and uneven pacing. Craig Allen Smith's energetic lead performance drives the show through its familiar story.
